questions.stem: A species that occurs naturally in Australia and nowhere else in the world is best described as:
options: naturalised in Australia
endemic to Australia
introduced to Australia
invasive in Australia
questions.explanation: An endemic species is native to one area and found naturally nowhere else. Introduced and naturalised species were brought in by people, and invasive describes an introduced species that spreads and causes harm.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines a native species of a region?
options: A species that occurs there naturally, without human introduction
A species that occurs only in that region and nowhere else at all
A species brought there by people that now breeds in the wild
A species that has spread there and harms the local ecosystems
questions.explanation: A native species belongs to a region naturally. Being found nowhere else makes a native species endemic as well, but many native species also occur naturally in other countries.

questions.stem: An introduced species is one that:
options: has been brought back to a region after it became locally extinct there
has spread through a region and reduced the numbers of native species
has been moved by people outside its natural range, on purpose or by accident
has evolved in a region and then spread naturally into neighbouring regions
questions.explanation: An introduced species reached its new area through human activity, deliberate or accidental. Reducing native species describes what an invasive species does, and not every introduced species does this.

questions.stem: The laughing kookaburra occurs naturally in eastern Australia. It was released by people in south-western Western Australia, where it now breeds in the wild. In south-western WA it is best classed as:
options: introduced, because people moved it outside its natural range
native, because it is an Australian species wherever it lives
endemic, because it is now found only in south-western WA
native, because it now breeds in the wild without human help
questions.explanation: Native status depends on a species' natural range, not on national borders, so an Australian species moved by people to another part of Australia is introduced there. Breeding in the wild makes it naturalised, not native.

questions.stem: Cane toads were brought to north Queensland in 1935. They have since spread across northern Australia and poisoned many native predators that try to eat them. In Australia the cane toad is best classed as:
options: endemic and invasive
introduced and invasive
introduced but not invasive
native but not endemic
questions.explanation: The toad was brought in by people, so it is introduced, and it has spread widely and harmed native species, so it is also invasive. It cannot be native or endemic, as it evolved in the Americas.

questions.stem: Wheat has been grown in Australia since early colonial times but rarely persists outside cultivated paddocks, and it does not spread into bushland. It is best classed as:
options: endemic to Australia only
introduced but not invasive
introduced and invasive
native but not endemic
questions.explanation: Wheat was brought to Australia by people, so it is introduced. It is not invasive because it does not establish and spread into natural ecosystems or harm them.

questions.stem: A shrub from southern Africa was sold in Australian nurseries. Fifty years later, surveys find it has spread from gardens into nearby bushland, where it forms dense stands that shade out native seedlings. How has its status changed?
options: From native to introduced and then invasive
From endemic to native but not endemic
From invasive to introduced but harmless
From introduced to introduced and invasive
questions.explanation: The shrub was introduced from the moment people brought it to Australia. Once it spread into natural areas and harmed native plants, it also became invasive; it can never become native, because its natural range is in Africa.

questions.stem: Which change to a river red gum floodplain is a change in an abiotic factor?
options: The spread of a fungal disease among the trees
The loss of the birds that pollinate the trees
Less frequent flooding because of upstream dams
The arrival of a new grazing herbivore in the area
questions.explanation: Abiotic factors are the non-living parts of an ecosystem, such as water, temperature, soil and light. A herbivore, a fungus and pollinating birds are all living, so changes in them are biotic.

questions.stem: Many heathland shrubs are killed by fire and regrow only from seed, and they need several years to mature and set seed. What is the most likely effect of fires every two or three years?
options: These shrubs decline, as they burn before setting enough seed
These shrubs increase, as each fire releases a new crop of seed
These shrubs are unaffected, as all heath plants are fire-adapted
These shrubs increase, as fire removes the grasses competing with them
questions.explanation: A fire regime is an abiotic factor, and frequent fire can wipe out species that need time between fires to rebuild a seed bank. Being adapted to fire does not mean being adapted to any frequency of fire.

questions.stem: The Bramble Cay melomys was a rodent found only on one low island in the Torres Strait. Researchers concluded it was lost after repeated sea-water inundation destroyed most of the island's vegetation. What kind of change was mainly responsible?
options: An abiotic change that made the island's soil too acidic for burrowing
An abiotic change that removed the food and shelter of an endemic species
A biotic change, as an introduced predator reached the island on a boat
A biotic change, as a disease spread to the island from the mainland
questions.explanation: Inundation by the sea is a change in a non-living factor, and it destroyed the vegetation the rodent depended on. Because the species lived on only one small island, a single local change could cause its loss.

questions.stem: During marine heatwaves on the Great Barrier Reef, corals expel the algae living in their tissues that supply much of their food, and many corals die. This is best described as:
options: a biotic change caused by an introduced species
an abiotic change caused by sediment run-off
a biotic change caused by the overfishing of reef fish
an abiotic change that disrupts a biotic relationship
questions.explanation: Water temperature is abiotic, and the relationship between corals and their algae is a biotic one. Run-off and overfishing also stress reefs, but the cause described here is heat.

questions.stem: Many small Australian mammals evolved over millions of years without placental predators such as foxes and cats. Why does this help explain why they have suffered so badly from these introduced predators?
options: They have never had any native predators of their own at all
They often lack behaviours that would help them avoid these hunters
They breed too slowly to survive any level of predation at all
They compete with foxes and cats for the same food plants
questions.explanation: Long isolation meant Australian prey did not evolve defences against hunters like foxes and cats, so the arrival of these predators was a new biotic pressure. They did have native predators, such as quolls, owls and snakes.

questions.stem: At an arid site, plots fenced to exclude only rabbits had 42 native shrub seedlings per 100 square metres after five years. Matching unfenced plots had 3. What is the most valid conclusion?
options: Native shrubs cannot regenerate anywhere in arid Australia unless fenced
Rabbit grazing greatly reduces native shrub regeneration at this site
Rabbits cause soil erosion that buries native shrub seedlings here
Fencing increased the rainfall inside the plots, raising germination
questions.explanation: Because the only difference between the plots was rabbit access, the gap in seedling numbers can be linked to rabbits, most likely through grazing. The data do not test erosion, and one site cannot support a claim about all of arid Australia.

questions.stem: Survey data from several wetlands show that as carp biomass increases, the water becomes more turbid and the cover of submerged plants falls. Which statement correctly classifies these two effects of carp?
options: Both effects are biotic, because carp are living organisms
Higher turbidity is biotic; loss of submerged plants is abiotic
Both effects are abiotic, because both happen in the water
Higher turbidity is abiotic; loss of submerged plants is biotic
questions.explanation: Turbidity is a physical property of the water, so it is abiotic, while plants are living, so their decline is a biotic effect. The cause being an animal does not make every effect biotic.

questions.stem: Carp feed by sucking up sediment and expelling what they do not eat. Which chain of effects best explains why native fish that shelter among water plants decline where carp are abundant?
options: Stirred sediment heats the water, which kills the native fish eggs directly
Stirred sediment adds oxygen to the water, which favours carp over natives
Stirred sediment lowers the salinity, which native fish cannot tolerate
Stirred sediment cuts light, submerged plants die back, and shelter is lost
questions.explanation: Suspended sediment blocks light, so submerged plants cannot photosynthesise well and die back, removing food and cover for small native fish. Carp also uproot plants directly as they feed.

questions.stem: Surveys show northern quoll numbers fell sharply at several sites in the year cane toads arrived. Which extra evidence would best show that the toads caused the decline?
options: Further counts of quolls at the same sites over the following ten years
Counts of how many cane toads were present at each of the survey sites
Records showing that quolls also eat many insects, frogs and small reptiles as prey
Dead quolls found with toads in their mouths, and stable numbers at toad-free sites
questions.explanation: Direct evidence of poisoning, plus matched sites without toads where quolls did not decline, rules out other explanations such as drought. More counts at the same sites would only confirm the correlation.

questions.stem: Field data near Alice Springs linked buffel grass invasion with higher fuel loads and more severe fires that killed woodland trees. Which effect of buffel grass is mainly an abiotic one?
options: A change to the fire regime, with more intense and severe fires
Displacement of the native grasses through competition for space
Loss of the plants that native seed-eating animals feed on
Death of the woodland trees and the animals that live in them
questions.explanation: Fire is a non-living factor, so changing how often and how intensely an area burns is an abiotic effect. Competition, food loss and tree deaths all concern living things, so they are biotic effects.

questions.stem: Before carp arrived, native fish made up 90% of the fish caught by mass in a river reach. Ten years later carp made up 75% and native fish 20%, and the total mass caught was about the same. Which interpretation is best supported?
options: Carp made up a smaller share of the catch than native fish did
The mass of native fish fell sharply as carp came to dominate the catch
The mass of native fish stayed the same, as the total did not change
Native fish increased, because carp provided them with a new food
questions.explanation: With a similar total, native fish falling from 90% to 20% of it means their actual mass fell to under a quarter of what it was. The unchanged total hides a large shift in which species make up the fish community.

questions.stem: Cane toads were deliberately released in north Queensland in 1935 in an attempt to:
options: control mosquitoes breeding in wetlands
provide a food source for native predators
control rabbits on coastal grazing land
control beetles damaging sugar cane crops
questions.explanation: Toads were brought from Hawaii to eat the larvae of cane beetles, which damage the roots of sugar cane. There is no evidence that they reduced the beetles, and they became a major pest themselves.

questions.stem: Which introduction of a species to Australia was unintentional?
options: European rabbits released near Geelong to be hunted for sport
Cane toads released in north Queensland to control the cane beetles
Cactoblastis moths released to control prickly pear infestations
Red imported fire ants arriving at Brisbane, probably in imported cargo
questions.explanation: Fire ants were found in Brisbane in 2001 and are thought to have arrived as stowaways in shipping cargo. The rabbits, toads and moths were all released on purpose.

questions.stem: The northern Pacific seastar is thought to have reached Tasmania's Derwent estuary as larvae carried in ships' ballast water. This is an example of:
options: an intentional introduction for aquaculture
an unintentional introduction through transport
an intentional introduction for biological control
a natural expansion of the species' native range
questions.explanation: Ballast water taken on in one port and released in another can carry larvae across oceans without anyone intending it. A natural range expansion would not involve human transport.

questions.stem: Eastern gambusia, small fish from North America, were brought to Australia in the 1920s to control mosquitoes. Studies have since found that they prey on the eggs and tadpoles of native frogs. What does this show about intentional introductions?
options: Introduced fish always fail to control the pest they were released for
Fish introduced to Australia can survive only in human-made ponds
Native frogs are harmed only by introduced species that are poisonous
A species released for one purpose can harm non-target native species
questions.explanation: Gambusia were meant to eat mosquito larvae, but as general predators they also eat frog eggs and tadpoles. This risk to non-target species is why biological control agents must now be tested before release.

questions.stem: Prickly pear once covered vast areas of Queensland and NSW. The moth Cactoblastis cactorum, brought from Argentina and released from 1926, destroyed most dense infestations. Why did this release succeed where the cane toad failed?
options: The moth was poisonous to eat, so no predator could reduce its numbers
The moth's larvae fed specifically on prickly pear, while toads ate many prey
The moth was native to Australia, so local species were adapted to it
The moth was released only in the areas where it had no native predators
questions.explanation: A successful biological control agent is host-specific, so it attacks the target and little else. The cane toad is a generalist that ate many native animals instead of controlling cane beetles.

questions.stem: Myxomatosis killed most rabbits it infected when it spread through Australia in the early 1950s, but later outbreaks killed a smaller proportion. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Rabbits learned to avoid the biting insects that carry the virus from rabbit to rabbit
The virus disappeared from Australia and was later released again in weaker form
Farmers stopped releasing the virus once rabbit numbers had fallen far enough
Natural selection favoured resistant rabbits, and less deadly virus strains spread
questions.explanation: Rabbits with inherited resistance survived and bred, while virus strains that killed hosts less quickly spread further, so the disease became less lethal over time. Learned avoidance is not inherited and does not explain the change.

questions.stem: In arid Australia, pastoral bores and dams provide permanent water. How do they favour introduced species such as feral goats and cane toads?
options: They raise soil salinity, which kills native plants before introduced ones
They attract native predators away from areas used by introduced animals
They cool the surrounding land, which suits species from colder climates
They let water-dependent animals survive and spread through dry country
questions.explanation: Many introduced animals need to drink often and could not otherwise survive in dry inland areas. Artificial water points remove this natural barrier, so excluding pests from them is one management option.

questions.stem: Many Australian native plants are adapted to soils low in nutrients such as phosphorus. Why do weeds often spread along bushland edges that receive fertiliser run-off from farms?
options: Fertiliser kills the insects that would otherwise eat the weeds' seeds
Run-off makes the soil saline, and only introduced plants tolerate salt
Fertiliser lowers the soil pH, which stops native seeds from germinating
Added nutrients favour fast-growing weeds over natives adapted to poor soils
questions.explanation: Many weeds come from fertile environments and grow quickly when nutrients are added, outcompeting slow-growing natives. Raising soil nutrients therefore changes an abiotic factor in a way that favours the invaders.

questions.stem: Why do introduced species such as rabbits, foxes and many weeds often thrive where native vegetation has been cleared or disturbed?
options: Cleared land has fewer abiotic factors for the species to cope with
Introduced species are unable to survive in undisturbed bushland
Clearing removes the diseases that would otherwise kill them
Disturbance opens up habitat and reduces competition from natives
questions.explanation: Clearing removes native plants and the cover native animals use, creating open conditions that many introduced species are suited to. Some introduced species, such as feral cats, also live in intact bushland.

questions.stem: How can roads and tracks built through bushland help introduced species to spread?
options: Verges act as open corridors for movement, and vehicles carry weed seeds
Road surfaces raise soil moisture, so introduced animals breed faster
Traffic kills native predators but not introduced animals on the road
Roads shade the ground nearby, which favours shade-tolerant weeds only
questions.explanation: Animals such as cane toads and foxes move easily along cleared roads and tracks, and seeds and soil on vehicles spread weeds and pathogens. Traffic kills both native and introduced animals.

questions.stem: Phytophthora cinnamomi, an introduced soil-borne pathogen, kills many plant species in the jarrah forests of south-west Western Australia. Which human activity most directly favours its spread?
options: Burning forest in cool, mild autumn conditions
Removing feral pigs that dig in the forest soil
Moving infested soil on vehicles, machinery and footwear
Planting jarrah seedlings in previously cleared farm areas
questions.explanation: The pathogen lives in soil and roots, so it spreads wherever infested soil is carried. This is why forests with dieback use vehicle wash-downs, boot-cleaning stations and track closures.

questions.stem: In managing invasive species, eradication means:
options: removing every individual of the species from an area for good
reducing the population to a level at which its harm is limited
reducing the harm the species causes without lowering its numbers
stopping the species from arriving in a new area in the first place
questions.explanation: Eradication is complete removal, so the species no longer exists in the area. Lowering numbers is control, lessening harm without lowering numbers is mitigation, and keeping species out is prevention through biosecurity.

questions.stem: Which strategy reduces the harm cane toads cause to native predators without reducing toad numbers?
options: Feeding quolls toad baits that make them ill, so they learn to avoid toads
Trapping and killing adult toads at breeding ponds each wet season
Removing every toad from an island before the population is able to breed
Collecting and destroying toad eggs and tadpoles in farm dams
questions.explanation: Conditioned taste aversion is a mitigation strategy: it changes predator behaviour so fewer are poisoned, while toad numbers stay the same. Trapping and collecting eggs are control, and removing every toad is eradication.

questions.stem: Rabbits, ship rats and house mice were all eradicated from Macquarie Island, which was declared free of them in 2014. Why is eradication usually more achievable on islands than on the mainland?
options: Islands have no native animals that baits could harm by mistake
Island pests cannot travel far, so all of them eat the first baits
Islands are isolated, so pests cannot easily reinvade once removed
Island pests breed more slowly, so their numbers fall faster
questions.explanation: Sea acts as a barrier, so once the last animals are removed the island stays pest-free if biosecurity is kept up. On the mainland, animals move back in from surrounding areas.

questions.stem: Before a new biological control agent is released in Australia, scientists test it against many native and crop species. What is the main purpose of this testing?
options: To confirm the agent comes from the same country as the target pest
To check it is host-specific and will not attack non-target species
To find out how quickly the agent can reproduce in captive colonies
To make sure the agent can survive in every Australian climate zone
questions.explanation: Host-specificity testing aims to avoid repeating mistakes such as the cane toad, which harmed many species other than its intended target. Surviving widely or breeding quickly does not make an agent safe.

questions.stem: Fox baiting in south-west Western Australia uses 1080 (sodium fluoroacetate). Why does it pose less risk to many native mammals there than to foxes?
options: Native mammals in the region are all herbivores, so none of them eats meat baits
Baits are laid only in winter, when native mammals in the region are hibernating
Native mammals evolved eating plants that contain fluoroacetate, so they tolerate it
Native mammals cannot smell the meat baits that are laid out to attract the foxes
questions.explanation: Fluoroacetate occurs naturally in native plants such as Gastrolobium, and animals with a long history of eating them have evolved tolerance. Foxes have no such history, so a small dose kills them; some native carnivores, such as quolls, are still at risk.

questions.stem: Which feature of a new invasive species incursion makes eradication most likely to succeed?
options: It is found early, while it is still small and contained
It is widespread, so baits can reach more individuals
It breeds rapidly, so its population drops faster when baited
It has spread into many different habitat types already
questions.explanation: Eradication becomes far harder and costlier as an invader spreads, because every last individual must be found. Early detection and rapid response give the best chance of complete removal.

questions.stem: In some reserves, baiting foxes without controlling feral cats has been followed by a rise in cat numbers and continued losses of small mammals. What does this suggest about managing invasive species?
options: Feral cats are native predators, so they increase whenever introduced foxes are taken away
Baiting foxes directly increases the breeding rate of small mammals' other predators
Small mammals decline because baits harm them more than foxes and cats ever did
Removing one introduced predator can release another, so they should be managed together
questions.explanation: Foxes compete with and kill cats, so removing foxes can let cat numbers grow and predation continue. Integrated programs target several pest species at once to avoid this.

questions.stem: Lantana forms dense thickets that shade out native understorey plants. It reduces native biodiversity mainly through:
options: competition for light and space
predation on native seedlings
spreading disease to native plants
hybridising with native shrubs
questions.explanation: By growing over and shading other plants, lantana outcompetes them for light and space. Predation and disease are other ways invasive species cause decline, but not the main way lantana does.

questions.stem: Researchers found that Australian mammal extinctions since colonisation began in the south-east, then spread to central and later northern Australia. Which evidence links them most strongly to foxes and feral cats?
options: The extinctions happened mostly in years of severe drought across the whole of the continent
The surviving species all live in rainforest, where foxes and feral cats have never reached
The pattern tracked the predators' spread, and some species survive on islands free of them
The extinct species were all large animals that people hunted for food and for their fur
questions.explanation: The timing and direction of the losses matched the spread of foxes and cats, and several species lost from the mainland persist on predator-free islands. Most of the lost species were small to medium-sized, not large hunted animals.

questions.stem: Many Australian mammals that have declined or become extinct weigh roughly 35 g to 5.5 kg, a pattern called the critical weight range. Which explanation is most often given?
options: Animals of this size need far more water than larger or smaller ones
Animals of this size were the main species hunted for their fur
Animals of this size are most affected by cold winter conditions
Animals of this size are the prey most often taken by foxes and cats
questions.explanation: Foxes and feral cats mostly hunt medium-sized prey, so species in this range have suffered most from them. Very small and larger mammals are taken less often.
